speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Goods and Services Tax (Amendment) Bill 2021 covers four sets of amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Two give effect to measures that were announced in the 2021 Budget Statement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The other two arise from our periodic review of the GST regime to clarify GST treatment and improve GST administration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOF sought views from the public on the draft Bill earlier this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The public consultation was conducted from 6 to 27 July 2021.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOF has published on 1 October 2021 our responses to the key feedback received.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have evaluated the feedback received and incorporated them where relevant and feasible to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We thank the contributors for their inputs which have allowed us to refine the amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We impose GST on all goods imported via land or sea, regardless of value.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also impose GST on goods imported by air or post with a value above $400.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We currently do not have GST on goods imported by air or post with a value of $400 and below.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is a gap which puts local businesses at a disadvantage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The extension of GST to such imported low-value goods and B2C imported non-digital services under these amendments will complement the GST that we already levy on business-to-business, or B2B, imported services, and on B2C imported digital services from 1 January 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Other jurisdictions have extended their GST or Value Added Tax, or VAT, similar to our proposed amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Jurisdictions that have extended their GST or VAT regimes to cover imported low-value goods include Australia, the European Union, New Zealand, Norway, Switzerland and the United Kingdom.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Similarly, jurisdictions which already tax B2C imported non-digital services include Australia and New Zealand.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The introduction of GST for low-value goods imported via air or post and for imported B2C non-digital services is necessary to ensure a level playing field for our local businesses and allow them to compete effectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Overseas suppliers of goods and services will be subject to the same GST treatment as local suppliers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These amendments will also keep our GST system resilient in a growing digital economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The legislative changes for the first set of amendments can be found in clauses 2 to 4, 6 to 15 and 17 to 26 of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Next, I will deal with the update on the GST treatment for a supply of media sales.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The second set of amendments updates the GST treatment for a supply of media sales.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Media sales refer to the sale of advertising space for hardcopy print and outdoor advertisements, advertising airtime for broadcasting via TV and radio, and web advertising via email, Internet or mobile devices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Currently, the basis for determining whether a supply of media sales is zero-rated or standard-rated depends on the place of circulation of the advertisement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If the media sales are circulated in Singapore, GST applies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If they are circulated abroad, then the supply of media sales is zero-rated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, this is no longer reflective of the state of media sales today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Online advertising has grown and is expected to account for an increasing share of advertising spending in future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Developments in digital technologies have changed the way that media sales are supplied and made it more difficult for suppliers of digital media sales to determine the place of circulation of the advertisement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, if the contractual customer of the media sales service belongs in Singapore, GST will be charged at the standard rate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This amendment is provided for in clause 11 of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Beyond these two sets of amendments, MOF regularly reviews the GST regime to clarify GST treatment and to improve GST administration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The first amendment arising from this periodic review updates the transitional rules for changes in GST treatment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For supplies spanning the date of a change in GST treatment, the transitional rules under the GST Act and Regulations help taxpayers determine whether the old or new GST treatment applies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Since then, there have been changes to our GST system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For instance, we introduced GST on imported B2B services and imported B2C digital services from 1 January 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have reviewed the transitional rules and updated them in consultation with the industry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the process of digitalisation and forced many brick-and-mortar stores to take their businesses online.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The learning curve has been a steep one and some are disheartened when they discover that after getting their store online, the challenges are far from over.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the past two years, we had observed a significant increase in interest in online shopping.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The borderless nature of the Internet would mean that Singaporeans also have easy access to foreign online marketplaces.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Local businesses would now find themselves competing with online sellers from overseas, who are often more experienced and able to offer their goods and services at lower prices due to lower production costs and lack of taxes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The business owners believe reducing the cost differences between buying products locally and overseas would, to some extent, help to drive the consumer traffic inwards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But to achieve its intended purpose, the policies must be pragmatic and enforceable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would GST be paid to the merchant or would consumers make the payment when their purchase reaches local customs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With this additional step of GST collection on an increased number of parcels, will this slow down the delivery process significantly?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How could a possible decrease in delivery service standards be mitigated, while ensuring prompt collection of taxes?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, if someone purchases a web design service from an independent designer overseas, is there any way for the authorities to track this transaction, besides self-declaration from the consumers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Government work with international payment platforms, such as PayPal and Stripe, to better monitor the outflow of online payments from Singapore to overseas?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some Singaporeans buy products from overseas that they cannot find locally.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They will now have to contend with significantly higher costs as a result of increasing shipping costs and GST costs and not to mention the supply chain disruptions that we are facing now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For the lower-income households, every cent in savings counts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Being driven towards local options that are initially more expensive than its foreign counterpart may be a win for the local retailer, but, for the low-income consumer, it would feel like a loss.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A resident of mine recently learnt to shop online after receiving training from the Seniors Go Digital Programme.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She has frequent backaches and was delighted to buy a brand of ointment from Indonesia, which is not available in any of the local supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She says it is much cheaper than her usual choice of ointment and more effective.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the new policy, she lamented that she may give up using it if it becomes too costly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I did tell her that she could try to suggest to some of our local supermarkets to bring in the product.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I understand, our local supermarkets and retailers have been heeding the Government’s call to diversify supplies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I would hope that our residents do not have to feel deprived of their favourite overseas products because it has become significantly costlier to purchase overseas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nonetheless, all this is happening in tandem with the scenario of a potential increase in local GST rates, which may take place by 2025.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singaporeans are still reeling from the economic impact of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, all these possible factors that may contribute to increased expenses may be very difficult to be taken as the normal scheme of things, even if the policy is necessary, and many countries have already implemented similar moves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A young resident tells me that he is feeling disheartened because he is still searching for a stable job after graduating, but costs of living are going up faster than he can find one.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The widespread popularity of e-commerce and foreign marketplaces in Singapore would mean that increasing GST not only impacts businesses, it also indirectly impacts Singaporeans’ costs of living.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is important that we address it as such.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With that said, I understand that some major multinational online marketplaces, in fact, already incorporate GST into their goods and services and pay it directly to the Government.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, the number of consumers affected by the new policy may be less than expected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, the Government should address concerns with regard to the impact of the policy on the cost of living in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Back then, I shared my concerns about the loss of public revenues through GST leakages and had also asked about the status of introducing GST on imported goods, a point which was first raised in Budget 2018.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I shared then that the OECD had, in March 2019, endorsed new rules and frameworks for the collection of taxes on the online sale of goods.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, COVID-19 has resulted in dual impacts on the retail sector in Singapore: firstly, an acceleration in the already rapid growth of the e-commerce market; and, secondly, the continued struggle of brick-and-mortar retailers amid an uneven playing field.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From the perspective of supporting our local SME retailers and to address a growing source of tax leakage due to overseas online retailers and to correct a key imbalance faced by tax-paying retailers in Singapore, I would like to state upfront that I am supportive of this Bill and the ensuing changes to ensure a level playing field for our local businesses to compete effectively.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A year ago, Finance Minister Lawrence Wong shared that he was very happy that I had brought up this point and supported it, because the MOF will certainly look for ways to raise more revenues and I believe the Minister will be equally happy with my discussion today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That being said, I do have a number of clarifications and broader issues to raise.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is that, since 1 January last year, GST is now payable on digital services provided by the GST-registered overseas service providers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In December 2019, IRAS shared that more than 100 overseas digital service providers have registered for GST under Singapore's Overseas Vendor Registration (OVR) regime and will be charging GST on their sales of digital services to Singapore consumers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Incidentally, Netflix has grown its subscriber base globally by about 1.5 times from 2018 to 2020, adding 37 million subscribers globally in 2020 alone.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, Disney+ was also launched in February this year, with many other over-the-top (OTT) services, Software as a Service (SaaS) and other forms of digital services witnessing prolific growth, due to the change in consumption patterns brought about by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More broadly, what has been MOF's initial assessment of the level of industry compliance, effectiveness of the administration of this tax and the number of cases of non-compliance by overseas vendors detected by IRAS so far?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In both of these cases, implementation is by way of extending the Overseas Vendor Registration (OVR) regime, similar to how GST was being extended to digital services.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Under certain conditions, a local or overseas operator of electronic marketplaces may also be regarded as the supplier of such low-value goods or imported services.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With the likes of Shopee and Lazada being the e-commerce marketplaces with the largest estimated market share here in Singapore and with these companies themselves being headquartered in Singapore, the focus on these popular electronic marketplaces and digital platforms does provide for an effective way to ensure tax compliance and proper GST collection.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, now that we are venturing into the realm of low-value goods, a significantly larger plethora of overseas businesses are now supposed to be GST-registered.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But the reality is that not all of them may be aware of this requirement and, even if they do, could simply decide not to go through this hassle to collect GST on the Singapore Government's behalf.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A quick search on the IRAS GST Registered Business Search throws up four records for Shopee, five records for Lazada, 20 for Amazon but none for Taobao, by far the most dominant marketplace in China, for example.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There could also be many more direct overseas vendors that may or may not be registered as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How then can IRAS ensure that there is a robust enforcement framework in place, to ensure that all those who fall within the scope of the OVR regime do so?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the absence of financial records of companies incorporated overseas, much less the amount of revenues they derive from Singapore specifically, how does IRAS make the determination as to which companies it seeks to audit or investigate?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And whether the overseas tax authorities will be able to provide as comprehensive an information set that IRAS seeks to retrieve?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The third point is in relation to one of tax efficiency and IRAS has been an efficient tax authority, a consistently low cost of tax collection at less than one cent per dollar of tax collected over the past years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And what is the cost of tax collection in this regard and the expected level of resources and costs to ensure a comprehensive compliance and enforcement framework?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The fourth point is more of an adjacent one and while Singaporeans may not be able to travel overseas as freely as we would like to right now, we do yearn for the skies one day.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As and when we do travel overseas, it is to be expected that one might be doing some shopping and bring home some gifts and souvenirs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Before I end, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I would like to speak about a number of broader but pertinent issues relating to GST.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party has been voicing our concerns on the GST hike since it was announced in 2018 and I take comfort that Member Mr Yip Hon Weng also shared his concern on the impending GST hike, where he pointed out in his speech on the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill last month, that this was originally announced before the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, Mdm Deputy Speaker, this impending GST hike is weighing on not just consumer confidence but also on businesses, especially the retailers hard-hit by COVID-19-related restrictions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Singapore Tenants United for Fairness group, for example, in commenting on the latest month-long extension of COVID-19 restrictions, shared that the frontline business community is in deep despair and disrepair, and I quote, "To make matters worse, over the next 12 months, frontline businesses will be further hit by a likely increase of GST to 9%".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The other factor that is critical to consider is that of inflation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: High inflation would simply mean lower real incomes and, at the moment, the debate globally, which has yet to be settled, is whether or not the current inflationary pressures in the market are seen to be transitory or permanent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What I do know, however, is that MAS is concerned enough about inflation to surprise the market with a tightening of monetary policy in October, that is, last month, given that external and domestic cost pressures are accumulating.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For Singaporeans already grappling with inflation and higher household expenditures, that additional two percentage points may be too much to bear.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yes, there will be the GST Assurance Package that delays and does not deny the impact of higher GST rates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yes, I acknowledge that there will be an enhancement to the permanent GST Voucher scheme, which, at the moment, only applies to those earning less than $2,300 a month, amongst other conditions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These may be progressive elements involved but does the raising of GST make our tax system as a whole more progressive or more regressive?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Do we really want higher GST to be the straw that breaks the camel's back?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I shared in my speech last year, we need to explore other forms of revenue sources before looking to an eventual GST hike to raise tax revenues.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Significant Infrastructure Government Loan (SINGA) Bill was passed earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We are now casting our GST net further overseas.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We are in the midst of the OECD global tax reforms which could, as Finance Minister Lawrence Wong pointed out, give Singapore some additional revenue.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And as I have shared during the Budget debates earlier this year, not all Government revenues are included in the official Budget.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must have the courage to make the difficult decisions that are necessary to uphold a culture of fiscal responsibility, even if it means walking back on a prior decision made under very different circumstances.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is not too late to change course and I strongly urge the Government to reconsider the necessity of a GST hike.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the past 20 months, due to the confluence of factors, such as travel restrictions due to the pandemic, the growth of end mile-delivery platforms, lower-priced alternatives and our digitally well-connected population, online shopping has become the norm for us Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since the onset of COVID-19, people have changed the way they shop and these changes are unlikely to reverse.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A recent study in Singapore last year by Visa also found that three in four consumers in Singapore are shopping online more frequently because of the pandemic and one-third of Singaporeans also made an online purchase for the first time.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The same survey also found that more than half of the respondents shopped less frequently in physical stores.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is likely due to the fact that we can purchase almost anything online now, from small, low-value items like cutleries, pots and pans, tools, mattresses and household items to expensive luxury items.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While most of us are enjoying the convenience of online shopping, a portion of our fellow Singaporeans, our small retail merchants, are struggling.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ms Ann Tan, a business owner at one of our neighborhood shops in Pasir Ris selling furniture, shared that her business has dropped by 50% and showed examples online where the overseas retailers were charging the same price for the exact same cupboards and shelves without GST.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Bike shops also shared examples where small bicycles parts like grips, handlebars and gloves were all available online from overseas but not subjected to GST.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The merchants also shared that some customers now are browsing the physical item in the shop, trying out the items, enquiring about the items but when it came to payment, some customers whip out their handphones and ask the shop owners for a lower price compared to what is available online.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The sale of these items used to be the bread-and-butter of our small retail merchants, but it is no longer.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With people shopping less frequently in physical stores and the unfair advantage that overseas suppliers have by not paying GST, our neighbourhood businesses are struggling to make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, our small retail merchants are hoping for a level playing field and the introduction of GST on low-value goods from overseas will be one of the enablers for that.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition to the introduction of GST on low-value goods from overseas, these small enterprises will need more assistance to remain competitive with the overseas online retailers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am glad that we have programmes like IMDA's SMEs Go Digital which has a three-step checklist to go digital and the retail industry digital plan which provides a step-by-step guide on the digital solutions for local retail SMEs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These programmes assist our small retail merchants to start their digital initiatives.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, most of them, at least for the small retailers in Pasir Ris, have found it hard to sustain the digital activities as they are usually a one- or two-man operation and have no resources nor skillsets to continue with these activities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   	The COVID-19 pandemic has changed our patterns of purchase drastically.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While many of us enjoy the convenience of online shopping, other Singaporeans, such as neighbourhood shop owners, clothes sellers and small businesses, are facing challenges in running their business.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of them have reported their business declining by 40% to 50% and one of the reasons was that prices of low-value items from overseas retailers are not subject to GST.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: By imposing GST on low-value items from overseas retailers, we can help our small retail businesses by balancing the opportunities for all traders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must also strive to continue helping our retail businesses to undergo digital transformation so that our small businesses can remain competitive in this increasingly challenging situation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mdm Deputy Speaker, the onset of COVID-19 has seen an irreversible shift in our patterns of purchase.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While many of us enjoy the convenience of online shopping, a portion of our fellow Singaporeans, our small retail merchants, are struggling to make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The introduction of GST on low-value items will help to level the playing field for our small retail merchants as, previously, low-value items from overseas retailers are not subjected to GST.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are truly challenging times for our neighbourhood small retailers and we have to do more to assist them on their digital transformation journey.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the proposal above, I support the amendments.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The same considerations that went into levelling the playing field for our marginalised families and residents would have gone into this new Bill, which also seeks to level the playing field for our local businesses when faced with the harsh inevitabilities of a globally open economy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we stumble upon tricky territory, as such developments necessarily produce winners and losers amongst our local businesses whether we like it or not, or whether we notice them or not.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The imposition of GST on the import of low-value goods is justified by a bid to support local businesses and we can infer by the pre-set $400 benchmark that the cost is intended to be passed on to consumers rather than businesses, reducing the attractiveness of low prices of suppliers abroad that were previously not subject to GST and, thereby, channeling demand locally.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The levelling of the playing field here is a welcomed move amongst our local retailers as they look towards the sustainable and necessary pivoting of their businesses in light of globalisation, e-commerce and changing consumer habits.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nothing says “local” like a home-based business, fuelled by the passions of Singaporeans, built from scratch in our own piece of Singapore property and incubated at their inception not by institutional investors, but by friends, family, loved ones and even neighbours.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Jia Jia never planned to become a home baker.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Out of her passion for baking, she started baking in her parents’ home and archived her creations on Instagram.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This attracted significant interest from friends and family, who enquired whether they could commission her to bake cakes for their parties and also make dessert boxes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Her consumer base grew gradually through word of mouth because of the popularity of her bakes and this allowed her to quit her full-time job to focus her attention on her passion-turned-livelihood in baking.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, she continues to run her bake sales on her Instagram and she has about 9,000 followers on her page.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Jia Jia’s home bakery can be seen as the epitome of local business – businesses with humble origins in Singapore, run by locals for locals.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of us have a Jia Jia in our lives, or a Jia Jia hopeful, particularly with the tail winds for local home-based businesses brought about by COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We may think that home-based businesses are supported because they are local, when, in fact, they are marginalised because they are small.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Not only is it unkind to expect home businesses to just die out because they are not scalable, but it is also presumptuous to think that home business owners necessarily intend on moving their businesses out of their homes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The home business owners I have spoken to believe they are "here to stay", insistent that their home-run businesses are what allows them to be personally involved in their passions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We cannot legislate taxation in a way that potentially invalidates the business models of home businesses if we want Singapore to really be where passion is made possible.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They keep their prices affordable not just to drive up profit margins, but because they thrive on strong personal relationships with the very people they serve.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Absorb the significant dent on profit margins passed on to them by GST and their businesses are in danger.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Pass it to their customers and they would feel that they have done them a disservice.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further, although it is desired that those affected by the GST on low-value imported goods would channel demand to the local economy, in the case of home business owners, this may not be so.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Once again, it must be reiterated that it has always been passion over prices.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our home business owners take a lot of pride in their work and put their heart and soul into their craft.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is one of the biggest draws of supporting home businesses.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: You know that your product has passed through the watchful eye of a personally invested business owner.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And this is why the home business owners I have spoken to maintain that they would never compromise on quality.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sometimes, this commitment to quality requires imports, such as for quality ingredients or materials that simply cannot be found in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This commitment to quality could pinch their profit margins should they continue to import their ingredients.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, Mdm Deputy Speaker, when debating on the tax on importing low-value goods, the question is not whether or not we should be #supportlocal.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The question is whether, by doing this, we are really supporting local.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would we be able to then further level the playing field through other support mechanisms for our home-based businesses, financial or otherwise, because our home-based businesses are often left unnoticed?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further, when debating the imposition of GST on imported goods, we must inspect the substantive benefits accrued to those we seek to uplift.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the peak of the restrictions last year, many Singaporeans were really quite dismayed to see the haunting photos of an empty Orchard Road and the impact on retailers in Singapore since then cannot be understated.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the rise of online shopping and e-commerce, some predict that online competition could spell the gradual debilitation of retail in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And this is a ghastly prediction the imposition of GST on low-value goods seeks to reverse.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While this is all done with good intentions, I believe we should not merely aim to prop up the retail sector in Singapore, but usher a new golden resurgence.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just as Times Square, Ginza, Tsim Sha Tsui, Dongdaemun crown the vibrancy of their world-class cities, it is time that Singapore polishes our crown and restores the vibrancy of our retail sector.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Merely levelling the playing field with price adjustments will serve us short term, but we cannot settle for stop-gap measures for what has once been the crowning jewel of urban life in Singapore, which is our retail sector.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This brings me to the case of Pazzion, best known as a brand for female footwear in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Any shop, online or brick-and-mortar, can peddle goods, but I would say brick-and-mortar shops are, at the moment, much better placed to deliver an experience.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is my hope that retailers and mall owners in Singapore can partner up to deliver retail experiences beyond the delivery of retail goods, rejuvenating the retail experiences for Singapore and her visitors.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is how we will truly be able to make the case for retail in Singapore to return to its crowning glory.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Online shopping makes purchases possible, but, here in Singapore, passion is made possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This ensures a level playing field for local suppliers and overseas suppliers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also commend the Ministry’s diligence in always providing summaries and its responses to key feedback received in its consultations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two points of clarification to make on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the GST treatment for the supply of media sales.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: IRAS’ e-Tax Guide has provided some guidance on how to identify the “direct beneficiary” of media sales.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, the e-Tax Guide provides that the contractual client will, generally, be regarded as the sole direct beneficiary where two conditions are satisfied.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, the service agreement does not require the services to be provided to another person.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the supplier liaises only with the contractual client and is accountable only to the contractual client.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if both conditions must be satisfied in order for the contractual client to be deemed the sole direct beneficiary?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Or is it sufficient that either one of the conditions is satisfied?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The e-Tax Guide also provides that when the two conditions are satisfied, the supplier does not need to look beyond the contractual client in determining the correct GST treatment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the event that the two conditions are not satisfied, can the Minister share what other factors a supplier should take into account to determine who the “direct beneficiary” of the service is?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, where multiple layers of contracts exist between a service provider and the beneficiary of a service, where should a supplier draw the line in determining its “direct beneficiary”?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the use of best available information to determine whether goods are distantly taxable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the public consultation conducted on the Bill, MOF had declined to accept a suggestion that the Bill prescribe information that businesses should rely on to determine if a supply of goods are distantly taxable goods that fall within the scope of GST.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOF declined to prescribe the information to reduce compliance burden and has stated that IRAS will provide examples in its e-Tax Guide.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the examples will be useful, what will also be important in the event of a dispute is which party bears the burden of proof.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate where the burden of proof lies and how the burden shifts in determining whether there was compliance with the tax treatment of distantly taxable goods?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, does the burden of proof shift to the Comptroller of Income Tax once the recipient is able to show a preliminary case that they relied on the best available information?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is the burden of proof then on the Comptroller to show that the recipient, in fact, had access to and should have relied on other information?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, it is important to ensure that our tax policies are reviewed and revised accordingly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It will also help to supplement the increased Government spending in the upcoming years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we need to provide more support for lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am concerned that imposing GST on all incoming overseas goods will lead to an increased burden on these residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Has the Government done research or sought feedback on how foreign online retailers intend to handle this tax increase?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If not, how much of it will be passed on to the consumers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As this new Bill mainly impacts individual buyers, the additional tax will be a heavier burden for our lower- to middle-income families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will be compounded by the impact of the GST hike that is likely to be implemented in the next few years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there further measures on top of the existing Assurance Package and GST vouchers to mitigate the impact on them?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Or can the quantum of these initiatives be increased to help families, given this new change?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will it be possible to utilise the Assurance Package or GST vouchers to cover online purchases, too?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we need to continue to encourage our local retailers to compete globally.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Compared to many of their overseas competitors, which have large economies of scale, SMEs are disadvantaged, as they often have to pay high rental and labour costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If the savings on purchasing foreign imports are reduced, this could diminish the attraction of overseas purchases, thereby encouraging more Singaporeans to support local businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, why do Singaporeans shop from overseas sites?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The second reason was the wider variety of international brands’ products and the lack of availability from local retailers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If Singaporeans cannot find their preferred brand, services or shopping experience locally, the imposition of the GST will do little to shift their buying behaviour towards local businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, local businesses must not be lulled into a false sense of security, thinking that they can rest on their laurels and become complacent with the perceived decreased competition from foreign markets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They must continue to innovate, use business analytics to understand their customers’ needs, establish global partnerships and bring in products that are in high demand.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government must continue to encourage and support our local businesses to compete globally by embarking on digitalisation and by getting onto these online retail platforms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this connection, perhaps the additional tax revenue from the imposition of GST can be funnelled to support the globalisation efforts of local businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With more companies and individuals obliged to comply with the new GST regime, compliance costs will, therefore, increase.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is the estimated number of low-value transactions in a year?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There may be a disproportionately large number of low- versus high-value transactions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, the Government may require disproportionately more resources to ensure that individuals comply with the new GST regulations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government ensure that there are adequate resources to enforce the new policies in an efficient manner?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will more personnel be hired to handle the additional workload at IRAS?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In light of the additional cost to ensure compliance, has any study been done to weigh up the cost of compliance, including prosecution of GST evasion, and the potential tax revenue that may be generated?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the new law, individuals are subjected to taxation or reverse charge.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is IRAS ready for the potential increase in enforcement action when this comes into play?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As for businesses, local GST is imposed on all GST-registered companies in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They collect GST from the customers or absorb it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And the collective amount is paid to the Government.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will foreign retailers who wish to sell to the Singapore market be GST-registered?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government engage these foreign businesses and provide them with the relevant legislative and administrative material, so that they have sufficient time to understand and apply the new practices?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps this ties in with my above point on compliance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are foreign companies with a large online shopping presence in Singapore, such as Amazon, Taobao and Lazada.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These companies allow smaller third-party companies to sell on their platform.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Have the relevant stakeholders engaged these companies to collaboratively resolve the issue of compliance?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What if the foreign retailer withholds GST payment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government deal with overseas companies who fail to comply with our GST regulations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the case of New Zealand, their Inland Revenue would monitor for non-complying retailers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is this an option that we would pursue?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Or will the burden then irrevocably fall on the customer as a reverse charge?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition, similar to Member Saktiandi Supaat's earlier point, how will consumers be made aware about whether their payment at the point of purchase already includes GST?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And will they be told that they have to pay additional GST to collect their parcel in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Unscrupulous merchants may leverage on this to cheat consumers into paying them a sum to retrieve their purchase.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Parcel clearance scams, where callers masquerade as customs officers asking for payment to retrieve a parcel, have not been uncommon even before this.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is thus imperative to educate consumers on when and where GST is to be paid and the official payment platforms to do so.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I would expect that SingPost or other online delivery platforms would be well-equipped by then to address more queries concerning GST payments on their parcels.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some packages may contain purchases from small businesses, or gifts from family and friends.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second-hand items like those from eBay, may have had their GST paid when the items were first bought.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are these second-hand items still subjected to GST taxation a second time?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is also not unheard of that some foreign retailers would allow customers to under-declare the value of their purchases to evade taxes, or to reduce the amount of tax payment due.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many firms now employ gig workers from overseas or outsource to provide remote services like designing programmes or media pieces.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such services are difficult to apply a quantum to and are easy to evade.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, many of these services could be under-declared or not declared at all, to avoid GST.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition, many of these small firms may neither have a turnover of $1 million nor are GST-registered.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will these firms – which may be acting as an underlying supplier or re-deliverer – be liable for reverse charge, if the services provided are below $400?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If reverse charge still applies to these firms, can they still pass these additional costs to the consumers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, the Government should provide some support to lower-income groups who are impacted by such taxes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Yio Chu Kang, I recall meeting Mdm K during a house visit, who was a homemaker looking after three kids.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Her husband, who is the sole breadwinner, is a delivery driver and does not earn a lot.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This policy is also an opportunity for our local businesses to innovate, in the face of a globalised world.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If local businesses are unable to improve their offerings and customer experience, they can expect our residents to continue shopping overseas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we do not innovate, we will stagnate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that the relevant agencies are well-equipped to handle the additional workload and customer enquiries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The policies must be well-enforced, with adequate information made accessible to the public, lest they become loopholes to be exploited for dishonesty and fraud.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) has to factor in many considerations and strike a delicate balance as it seeks to fulfil its mission.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, there is the trade-off between protecting revenue and minimising the distortions of taxes on market competition.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, it has to find ways to optimise the efficiency of tax administration and avoid unnecessary enforcement burden.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But I can see why the Ministry is implementing GST on this category of goods.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is no better time to start than this current moment and e-commerce has become the hottest vertical in Singapore's tech sector during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In other countries, e-commerce platforms collect and remit the tax on the Government’s behalf, as they take on the role of a "store" with an offering of different supplies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In many cases, it acts as the sole point of contact with the end consumers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Under our current Overseas Vendor Registration regime, I understand that foreign suppliers and e-marketplace operators which make significant sales of digital services to Singapore’s consumers are required to register with IRAS for GST.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With this new legislation, the Overseas Vendor Registration regime will be expanded.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Singapore-based purchasers, like the consumers, be asked to pay for the GST?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can IRAS work with Electronic Distribution Platforms (EDPs), like Aliexpress and eBay, via a joint and several liability (JSL) notice mechanism to notify the foreign suppliers, as we are unable to regulate these suppliers effectively, to help us with the tax collection?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: IRAS should concentrate its efforts in the fight against GST fraud and ensuring the effective taxation of cross-border online sales to raise additional revenue and strengthen the functioning of our tax systems.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand the need to grow our tax base in order to fund other expenditures.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):    One of the justifications for levying of GST on low-value imported goods sold online is to ensure fair competition for our domestic retailers against online retail platforms.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singaporean retailers are required to charge GST on their sales, but online retailers are not.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While this measure may help some of our local stores narrow the price gap between them and online retailers, our consumers will have to pay higher prices.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Due to the pandemic and the Government's persuasion, many Singaporeans have changed their shopping habits.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Cautious consumers should not be punished for remaining wary of crowded shopping centres and stores, especially as COVID-19 cases and hospitalisations are on the rise again.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, local retailers who have supplemented their business with online sales may face the double whammy of low footfall plus a new tax on their online sales of imported items.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, I have some questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is this new approach meant to minimise the entry of high numbers of new gig economy operators, like the SMEs, into the GST system, perhaps with limited compliance capacity and knowledge of their tax obligations?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am concerned that the new economy operators, especially the micro-businesses and SMEs, may often have limited GST knowledge and capacity to comply while their activities may involve considerable GST revenues and create risks of competitive distortion that may be significant at an aggregated level.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Does IRAS expect the revenue impact of this approach to be significant when activity shifts from a limited number of established and largely GST-compliant conventional operators to a large number of gig economy operators that may remain outside the scope of GST?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will bringing in these new gig economy operators into the GST net create undue pressure on tax administration and compliance challenges for the operators?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will IRAS use technology to facilitate GST administration and compliance?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are there third-party reporting obligations, taxpayer education and other activities to raise awareness?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How does IRAS enforce and collect the right amount of tax?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The purchases that many Singaporeans purchase online are less than $400.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, many Singaporeans will be affected and feel that they are forced to pay the cost of COVID-19 even though the change will only happen in 2023.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Online sellers have found ways to evade paying taxes: posting goods without declaring, offering services on online social media, boosting cash transactions and running multiple sales websites.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I look forward to the Minister's response and would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The questions raised by the Members fall broadly into four categories.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, how IRAS will implement GST on low-value goods imported via air or post and business-to-consumer, or B2C, imported non-digital services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, how IRAS will enforce collection and ensure compliance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Third, specific queries on the updated GST treatment for a supply of media sales.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Fourth, feedback concerning cost of living and the GST Voucher Scheme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Don Wee and Mr Louis Ng asked how GST on low-value goods imported via air or post and B2C imported non-digital services will be implemented.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These regimes are not new and have been successfully implemented from 1 January 2020 to tax business-to-business, or B2B, imported services and B2C imported digital services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will collect GST from their customers on such supplies and then hand the collected GST over to IRAS.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Non-GST registered customers in Singapore include individuals like many of us here.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This approach ensures a level playing field in terms of GST treatment, whether we buy such services or goods from local suppliers or overseas vendors Mr Don Wee asked whether a simplified registration and compliance regime will be available for overseas vendors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Overseas vendors can already choose to register under a simplified pay-only mechanism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The simplified pay-only mechanism allows overseas vendors to enjoy simplified GST reporting and documentation requirements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our RC regime does not affect most GST-registered entities in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is how we keep the tax compliance burden low.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is because they are fully taxable persons entitled to a full refund on the GST incurred on their purchases and even their account for GST on the low-value goods imported by air or post or on imported services, they will still get a refund of this same amount.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Only a small minority of GST-registered entities here are subject to RC – these make non-taxable supplies, such as exempt supplies or non-business supplies, and cannot get a full refund of GST incurred on their purchases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This minority of GST-registered entities that are subject to RC include financial institutions and residential property developers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For this minority of GST-registered entities that are subject to RC, they are required to account for GST on the imported services, including services procured from overseas gig workers, regardless of the value of the services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is similar to how we do not require local businesses with less than $1 million annual turnover to register for GST.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how, under OVR, consumers will know if their payment at the point of purchase already includes GST and how Singapore Customs will know if GST has already been paid on a package.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When consumers check out their purchases, GST-registered overseas vendors will charge and collect GST on the low-value goods at the point of purchase when the order is confirmed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is similar to how, since 1 January 2020, GST is collected on imported B2C digital services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where GST has been charged and collected by the overseas vendor on the low-value goods, the overseas vendor will include the relevant information on the GST collected in the commercial document which is passed through the logistics chain.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Import GST will not be payable at the border when this information is furnished to Singapore Customs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, for goods delivered via air couriers, the GST registration number of the overseas vendor is included in the summary list of parcels to be imported or in the permit declared to Singapore Customs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how GST-registered entities that are subject to RC can use best available information to determine if a purchase is subject to RC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As I have explained earlier, only a small minority of GST-registered entities here are subject to RC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When these entities buy low-value goods, RC will apply only if the goods are imported by air or post into Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Singapore Customs already collects GST for all goods imported via land and sea into Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: GST-registered entities that are subject to RC will usually know from its contract with a supplier whether the low-value goods it buys is located outside Singapore at the point of sale and whether the goods will be imported via air or post.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, there may be occasions in which the GST-registered entity only knows this information upon receipt of the goods.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Allowing GST-registered entities that are subject to RC to use the best available information to determine whether the RC applies is, therefore, meant to ease compliance by such entities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Apart from information available at the time of purchase of the goods, the entities can use information at the point of goods receipt or other information collected by their business systems and processes to determine the location of goods and mode of shipment into Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One example of such available information is the import and shipping documents that accompany the goods.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As it would be difficult to envisage all the types of available information that may be used, we will not provide a prescriptive list of information that GST-registered entities subject to RC can rely on.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Instead, IRAS will provide examples on the type of documents or information in its e-Tax Guide.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Entities subject to RC can approach IRAS for clarification if they wish to use other available information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Don Wee, asked how we will engage overseas vendors and ensure that they comply with the new GST regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This has helped IRAS gain experience in administering and enforcing the regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The rules of our OVR regime are consistent with those of other jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This makes it easy for overseas vendors to comply and also provides certainty for the industry.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Many of these overseas vendors are familiar with similar GST or VAT obligations in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are not the first jurisdiction to implement GST on low-value goods imported via air or post, or on imported services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For instance, Australia, the European Union, New Zealand, Norway, Switzerland and the United Kingdom have extended their GST or VAT regimes to cover low-value goods.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our experience with OVR thus far since 1 January 2020 and the experience of other jurisdictions with OVR show that these multinational businesses do comply with GST or VAT obligations of the jurisdictions they make supplies to.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IRAS will make use of various information sources to identify and engage overseas vendors that should be GST-registered and verify their GST reporting after GST-registration.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the event of non-compliance, the existing penalty and enforcement regime under the GST Act will apply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IRAS is empowered to raise additional tax assessments, apply penalties and recover the outstanding tax payable directly or through the appointment of agents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Provisions in bilateral tax agreements will also allow IRAS to obtain information on overseas vendors from other tax jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IRAS has been actively engaging the industry, including overseas vendors, on the implementation details for the OVR and RC regimes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include consultation on IRAS' draft e-Tax Guides and the proposed legislation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IRAS is also conducting outreach activities for potential GST registrants, including participating in workshops in various international fora and holding webinars, to educate overseas vendors on the new GST rules.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will now proceed to address questions regarding the updated GST treatment for suppliers of media sales.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Currently, the GST treatment depends on where the advertisement was circulated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With the advent of the digital economy, including online advertisements, our GST treatment needs to be updated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IRAS has provided guidance in its e-Tax guide to state that the person who contracts for the service, or the contractual client, will, generally, be regarded as the only person who directly benefits from the service, where two conditions are satisfied.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first condition is that the service agreement does not require the services to be provided to another person.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second condition is that the supplier of the service liaises only with the contractual client and is accountable only to the contractual client.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether both of these conditions must be satisfied, in order for the contractual client to be deemed the sole direct beneficiary and how to determine the GST treatment of the supply of media sales in the event that both conditions are not satisfied.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IRAS has provided examples in its e-Tax guide to illustrate this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where the two conditions are not satisfied, the determination of the direct beneficiary would be dependent on the facts of the case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As a general rule, the supplier should consider the party other than the contractual client stated in the contract that he is required to provide a service to and to whom he is accountable for his service deliverables.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In both instances, the supplier will have contact with the subsidiary in Singapore, the actual recipient of his service.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Therefore, regardless of the presence of multiple layers of contracts, the supplier will know the direct beneficiary of his supply of service.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IRAS will include more examples in its e-Tax guide to illustrate the situation where both of these conditions are not satisfied.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This, in turn, levels the playing field for our local businesses, as overseas suppliers of goods and services will be subject to the same GST treatment as local suppliers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This change also helps to defend our GST revenue base from being eroded as the digital economy grows and more people shop online.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked whether the tax revenue from this measure could be used to provide more support to small retailers and help with their digital transformation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are schemes already in place, such as SMEs Go Digital, Heartlands Go Digital and SME centres, to help small retailers through ground support and consultancy services with their digital transformation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling called for more support for microbusinesses and wider changes to support our retail ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have implemented several schemes throughout 2020 and 2021 to help SMEs in the retail sector.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are also refreshing the Retail Industry Transformation map, or ITM, which lays out a longer-term vision for the industry as part of a broader refresh of the 23 ITMs, given disruptions brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how this measure would impact overall inflation and living costs in Singapore, particularly for the lower- and middle-income.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The bulk of individual consumption, such as food, utilities, transport, education and health care, will not be affected by the change.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These goods and services are, typically, bought from local suppliers rather than from overseas suppliers and thus are not affected by the extension of GST to low-value goods imported via air or post and B2C imported non-digital services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked whether additional assistance will be provided on top of the Assurance Package and GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have said that the Government will continue to absorb GST on publicly subsidised healthcare and education.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To support lower-income Singaporeans, we already have other permanent schemes, such as Workfare Income Supplement (WIS), Silver Support and ComCare.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As part of our annual Budget, we have also provided additional support, such as Service and Conservancy Charge (S&CC) rebates and top-ups to Child Development and Edusave accounts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government remains committed to supporting Singaporeans, with more help given to the lower-income.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He had also asked about the number of cases of non-compliant overseas vendors under the existing OVR regime detected by IRAS so far.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IRAS has not detected any cases so far and the overseas vendors are generally compliant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He had asked how much does the Government expect to collect from each of the new measures.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And his final question was whether there will be any changes to GST import relief for those coming back from overseas.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think Mr Louis Chua then concluded by a call to review whether or not it is necessary to raise the GST rate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First of all, today is not really the time to have a debate on whether or not we should raise GST as a whole, because today's Bill is focused on a very specific aspect, which is low-value goods.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, I want to just make a few general remarks, given that Mr Louis Chua has also made a call or some remarks on raising of the GST rate, which is really this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You have to consider our revenue and you have to consider our expenditure situation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I think Members of the House know this already.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In terms of our revenue, taxes and fees are only 80% of our total revenue.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are already relying on the NIRC for 20%.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our revenue is not coming from taxes alone.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the budgetary surpluses of the entire last two decades have been called upon because of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And because of COVID-19, because of the pandemic, we have had to dig into our reserves – not just NIRC, but the actual reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the draw on our past reserves amounted to about $53 billion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is our revenue situation – we are digging into the savings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the other hand, our expenditure, if you just look at the horizon – and I outlined this in my speech yesterday on the Adjournment Motion – we have very large expenditure items looming on the horizon.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have a situation where our fiscal situation is already tight, because we are digging into our savings and our reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have got impending challenges which require us to spend more and you also have the Workers' Party, on top of that, asking us to spend even more than that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Workers' Party has attempted to put forward some suggestions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, they have suggested tax increases; they support the tax change today.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But you must remember that the kind of money that is raised from the GST change in today's Bill is in the millions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if there is a GST increase of two percentage points, the amount of revenue raised per year is about $3 billion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the kind of expenditure that is required is billions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The other suggestion that the Workers' Party has put forward is on land sales and to treat land sales as revenue.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You have just converted it from a physical form to a cash form.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is just not prudent in terms of the way one should run a fiscal system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I would just simply urge the Workers' Party to consider this: our fiscal constraints, the need to spend more and that the money must come from somewhere.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I had also, yesterday, outlined why the Singapore system – the taxation system and the fiscal system – is progressive and fair.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is built on principles that everybody contributes something, but those who have more contribute more.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, in some cases, a lot more.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And what we do is we redistribute it to those who have less.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Tourism is down now, but when you look at the mid- and longer-term projections, that 60% still remains the same.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, our GST system is a good example of how we do this redistribution and never forget that this Government will do what is necessary to support our people.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Every time the MTF had to put in place measures that affect businesses, we put in place support.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, you cannot look at just one single item and say, "Oh, this, by itself, please change, it is very onerous".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You do have to look at the bigger picture.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And you cannot just look at a very narrow tunnel-vision thing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is all I plan to say about GST at this stage and I hope that this is something that the Workers' Party will reflect on.
